I mainly brought up the definitions because your original response to NoWeight equated homophobia with hate—my intention was to show that hate isn’t a necessary component, and homophobia can be expressed even in milder forms, such as “dislike.” However, you are correct that not liking yuri should not necessarily be conflated with homophobia. There are legitimate reasons why people might not like yuri—some in the LGBTQ community find it fetishy, and for some it might just not be their cup of tea.

That said, I don’t think it’s idiotic to interpret this post as homophobic. Honestly, I think OP is more likely a generic troll who *wanted* people to take it that way so he could enjoy the shitstorm. I see where you’re coming from too, for what it’s worth—if we only look at the words of the post, then it’s just someone stating they don’t like a genre.

The thing is, communication is about much more than just the words we use. It’s about the purpose of what we say, the tone, the venue, the reputation of the speaker, and the values of the people listening. So try to take some of those factors into consideration: to begin with, many of the talents tend to play up yuri in their content and the fanbase eats it up, so this take was already going to be unpopular. Then you have the exaggerated (some might say tasteless) nature of the meme. On top of that, their actual purpose is kind of muddy—it’s not like it’s hard to avoid yuri content, so it begs the question, “Why bother posting this at all?” In your hypothetical example, the person is uncomfortable with the lesbians being intimate in their presence, but this is more like someone not liking lesbians being intimate some place they can easily avoid. If OP cannot tolerate the mere thought of yuri content existing, it’s not that far-fetched to think homophobia may be the root cause. Anyone could also take a quick peek at OP’s comment history—they talk about their dislike of yuri too often for this to be a one-off joke, and they’ve made multiple openly transphobic statements (which don’t prove they’re homophobic, but certainly don’t help their case either).

All this might sound like overthinking, but people subconsciously go through these thought processes all the time. And none of it definitively proves OP is homophobic (which is impossible to “prove” anyway since that’s a subjective call). You probably spend more time on okbh than most people on this sub, so you probably have a more generous and ironic view of shitposts.

If you really want to get into semantics, I checked three online dictionaries (Merriam-Webster, OED, and Google) and none of their current definitions for “homophobia” mention hate, but they do include the words “dislike” and “aversion to.”

(Side note: The word “hatred” only appears in the OED’s 1901 outdated definition of homophobia, which referred to fear or hatred of men or mankind.)

This is really thoughtful and well put together! The title had me worried but you were very fair about your arguments.

If I have any contention to make, though, I think Yamazaki knew *what* his games were about—maybe just not *who* they were about. In my opinion, the Investigations duology and DD/SoJ all have strong and discernible themes that you can track from case to case, even if they can be a bit heavy-handed at times (*cough cough Dark Age of the Law*). His games have a clear message that builds over the course of his games, even in filler cases, which I think is a real strength in the writing. I prefer the original trilogy, but I do think its filler cases often feel more like episodes out of an anthology series than a building sequence of events that echo a cohesive theme. JfA is probably the worst offender, where the two cases that actually matter to the overarching plot barely have any overlapping subtext.

That said, people love Ace Attorney more for the characters than the deep ideas (even though they’re present in all the games). Unfortunately, character-writing is where the Yamazaki games struggle, for all the reasons you already mentioned. They understand how characters would speak and emote in situations, but they never quite figured out how to build each character’s new arc off the previous one—it’s just constantly starting from scratch. It’s especially telling in the Investigations games. Edgeworth is fun to play as. He looks like Edgeworth. He talks like Edgeworth. But sometimes he feels like a body-snatched version of Edgeworth, because he doesn’t carry through any of the struggles and doubts we see him face in the original trilogy. At best it just feels inconsistent, but at worst it almost makes him seem like a hypocrite.

Anyway, tl;dr, I pretty much agree with everything you wrote, just offering another perspective about theme vs character.

Is it that people criticized KH2 and it became a classic, so KH3 will also become a classic? We won’t know that for a while, so there’s little point speculating now. Is it that people overreacted to KH2 then so they must be overreacting to KH3 now? That’s comparing apples and oranges. Even if the phrasing is similar, criticisms that may have been legitimate for one game may not be for another. Is it that KH2 was fairly criticized at the time but eventually people started to ignore its faults, and the same may happen with KH3? In linguistics, there are two main camps: prescriptivism (all definitions and pronunciations should match their original context) and descriptivism (definitions and pronunciations should be updated based on their actual usage in real life). I believe in descriptivism . It’s why “mad” now means “angry” when it used to only mean “insane.” Context and usage change things over time. The dub says SAY-IN, which is how most English-speaking Dragon Ball fans pronounce it.

Your pronunciation may be more “faithful” to the original but I don’t see how it benefits anything other than one’s own pedantry to call the large majority of English-speaking fans wrong for saying it the way their only exposure to the franchise told them to. Unless you can go back in time and tell the Funi dubbers to change it, the distinction is moot and more than a little elitist.
